7	
8	# DAR is one generated Unified Star Schema: an event bridge whose stages own their measures and inherit only keys, one peripheral per entity, one dense calendar
9	
10	## Context and Problem Statement
11	
12	DAR is the layer a person reads. The blueprint says it is volatile and generated (R4), and the
13	Unified Star Schema is the shape chosen for it: one *bridge* holding a row per measurement event,
14	one *peripheral* per entity holding its current state, and one calendar every process is dated
15	against. This record fixes what the generator emits, because every question, every page and every
16	future consumer is written against those column names and will not survive them changing.
17	
18	Three things about the source make the shape less obvious than the description sounds.
19	
20	**Fan-out.** The USS description says keys and measures propagate downward along many-to-one
21	relationships. Keys can. Measures cannot: if a parent's measure were copied onto every child row
22	that points at it, summing that measure would multiply it by the number of children. That is the
23	classic fan trap, and avoiding it is the entire reason a bridge exists rather than one wide join.
24	
25	**History.** DAB keeps a version of every entity row. A question about something that *happened*
26	and a question about a state as it was *observed* are different questions and need different rows,
27	but they belong in one table, because the whole value of the bridge is that two processes can be
28	summed and compared on one calendar.
29	
30	**What the generator is allowed to read.** Two observations constrain this hard, and both were
31	made against the real engine on DuckDB rather than reasoned about. `<entity>_focal` and
32	`<entity>_idfr` are created but never populated — a generator that joined to them would produce
33	empty results and no error. And `view_<entity>_with_rel` carries no relationship key columns at
34	all, despite its name; its column list is byte-identical to `view_<entity>`. A generator built on
35	the names alone would be wrong in both directions.
36	
37	There is a fourth thing, and it is the one this slice cannot demonstrate. The argument that one
38	shared bridge is safe rests on the walk over many-to-one edges. Slice 1 has one entity and no
39	relationships, so the walk has zero edges and nothing inherits. The property is asserted here and
40	first exercised in slice 2.
41	
42	## Decision Drivers
43	
44	* a `sum()` over the bridge is right without the reader knowing how the model is shaped
45	* one calendar, so two processes can be compared
46	* a published column contract that a model change *extends* rather than rearranges
47	* deterministic output: the same declarations always produce the same SQL
48	* nothing silently missing
49	
50	## Considered Options
51	
52	* An event bridge with one stage per (entity, event), keys inherited and measures owned
53	* One bridge row per entity instance, with measures joined on
54	* A hand-written star schema per question
55	* Reading DAB's relationship views for the inherited keys
56	
57	## Decision Outcome
58	
59	Chosen option: **an event-grained bridge whose stages own their measures and inherit only keys.**
60	
61	*Keys inherit; measures do not.* A stage carries the key of every entity it reaches by walking
62	many-to-one edges, and a measure is non-null only on the stage of the (entity, event) that owns
63	it. Every other branch of the union emits a typed `NULL` in that column. This is what makes
64	`sum()` additive at any grain the reader chooses, and it is proved by a test rather than trusted:
65	a fixture with two parents and three children, where `sum(_measure__parent__…)` must still be the
66	parent total and not three times it.
67	
68	*One row per measurement event.* A transaction stage reads `dab.view_<E>_hist`, keeps the latest
69	version in which the event's date is set, and dates the row by that attribute. An unshipped order
70	therefore has no shipment event *by construction* rather than by a filter somebody has to
71	remember. A state stage reads the same history view, dates rows by `eff_tmstp`, and marks the
72	latest version per key `_is_current`. Both kinds land in the same table with the same columns,
73	which is what lets them be compared.
74	
75	*The generator reads `view_<entity>_hist` and the relationship pair objects, and nothing else.*
76	Not `_focal`, which is empty. Not `_with_rel`, which does not carry what its name implies. Reading
77	the current view instead of the history view would also lose `_observed_at`, which is how a bridge
78	row carries its own provenance back to the DAS load that produced it.
79	
80	The rejected options each fail on one of the drivers. One row per entity instance with measures
81	joined on is the fan trap, restated as a design. A hand-written star per question abandons R4 and
82	puts the layer's correctness in a person's hands, every time, forever. Reading the relationship
83	*views* rather than the pair objects is the subtle one: those views rank pairs by effective
84	timestamp and keep the open rows, and our effective timestamp is the moment DAS observed the row,
85	so a changed foreign key can drop out of the view entirely — rows silently missing from the
86	bridge, with the query still running and the total merely smaller.
87	
88	### The column contract
89	
90	`dar__uss._bridge`:
91	
92	| column | type | null | meaning |
93	|---|---|---|---|
94	| `_stage` | VARCHAR | no | the entity this row is a row *of* |
95	| `_event` | VARCHAR | no | the event, lower-cased: `placed`, `shipped`, `observed` |
96	| `_event_date` | DATE | no | the day it happened, or the day the state was observed; joins `_calendar.date_key` |
97	| `_is_current` | BOOLEAN | no | always true on a transaction stage; the latest version per key on a state stage |
98	| `_observed_at` | TIMESTAMP | no | the DAB `eff_tmstp` behind this row, which is the DAS `extracted_at` |
99	| `<entity>_key` | VARCHAR | own key no, inherited yes | one per entity in model order |
100	| `_measure__<entity>__<measure>` | BIGINT for a count, DECIMAL(28,8) for a sum | non-null only on the owning stage | one per declared measure, in model order |
101	
102	`dar__uss.<entity>` is a peripheral **table**, one row per key, key first and attributes in
103	declaration order. Tables rather than views, so what DAR served is exactly what the build log
104	describes.
105	
106	`dar__uss._calendar` is dense and daily from the first to the last `_event_date` in the bridge,
107	with civil arithmetic only — `year_number`, `quarter_of_year`, `month_of_year`, `day_of_month`,
108	`year_start`, `quarter_start`, `month_start`, `quarter_label`, `month_label`. Column names avoid
109	reserved words. Fiscal periods and holidays are business meaning and would need a definition, so
110	they belong in DAB and not in a generator.
111	
112	Two rules follow from the contract and are written down because they are query-time traps: a join
113	on the row's own stage key may be `INNER`, a join on an inherited key must be `LEFT`; and a ratio
114	is `sum(a) / sum(b)` at query time, never a stored measure.
115	
116	Nulls: the generator never invents a member. A null dimension stays null, and a question that
117	wants nulls grouped or excluded says so in the question file, where that choice belongs.
118	
119	### Consequences
120	
121	* Good, because a sum over the bridge is additive whatever the shape of the model, and the proof
122	  is a test rather than a convention
123	* Good, because every process lands on one calendar, so two of them can be compared
124	* Good, because a consumer writes against a contract that a model change extends — new entities
125	  and measures are appended, never inserted or renamed
126	* Good, because a changed foreign key keeps its row, which reading the relationship view would not
127	  have done
128	* Bad, because the bridge is sparse: most cells of most rows are null. At this scale that costs
129	  nothing, and it is the price of one table instead of one per process
130	* Bad, because ratios and state questions need care at query time, and nothing in the schema stops
131	  a reader averaging an average
132	* Bad, because this slice cannot demonstrate the property the shared-bridge deviation (D-0001)
133	  rests on. With one entity there are no edges to inherit along, so the fan-trap argument is
134	  carried on assertion until slice 2
135	* Bad, because the generator now depends on three specific behaviours of a third-party engine on a
136	  platform that engine does not advertise supporting. Each is pinned by a check, but a vendor
137	  change could invalidate any of them
138	
139	### Confirmation
140	
141	A machinery test asserts the column order, the event-date filter and the refusals — including
142	that a **zero-edge walk is a valid walk**, so slice 2 does not meet that as a special case. A
143	second asserts that every branch of the union emits the contract columns **in the contract
144	order**, which is stronger than aliasing each once and is the assertion that matters: a union
145	takes its column names from its first branch, so a branch that emits the right columns in a
146	different order puts one measure's values silently into another measure's column, and `DESCRIBE`
147	still matches. Every emitter's output, laid out the way the generator lays it out, is run through
148	the repository's own linter.
149	
150	Data checks pin the engine behaviours this design rests on, so a vendor change says so rather
151	than quietly emptying the star schema: that `_focal` and `_idfr` are still empty; that
152	`view_<E>_with_rel` is still a passthrough on a relationship's *source* side and gains exactly
153	the source entity's columns on its *target* side; and that `v_<edge>` still hands over the raw,
154	unranked pairs. The `with_rel` check first asserted the passthrough of *every* entity, which was
155	true only while there were no relationships — ADR 0006 corrects the observation, and this
156	section now describes the check that exists. A fourth asserts `DESCRIBE dar__uss._bridge`
157	equals the plan on the real warehouse, and a fifth counts the description table directly, which is
158	the only place an ingestion-strategy defect is visible.
159	
160	**The fan-out test exists as of slice 4**, in `tests/test_fan_out.py`. It **could have existed in
161	slice 2**, and this section said otherwise: it claimed the test needed two grains the system did
162	not yet have. The test runs entirely on the neutral fixture, and that fixture gained a CHILD with
163	its own measure in slice 2, at the same time as the first relationship. What was missing was not a
164	second grain but the decision to go and build one; the excuse was wrong and the two slices of
165	delay were real. It runs the
166	generated SQL over a two-grain warehouse and asserts that a parent's measure is its own total and
167	not its children times it; ADR 0012 records what it covers, what mutation makes it fail, and the
168	half of D-0001's argument it shows to be false.
169	
170	`adss dar generate --check` regenerates and fails on any diff, which is what keeps the committed
171	SQL from becoming a second truth.
172	
173	This decision is the argument behind deviation **D-0001** in
174	[deviations.md](../deviations.md).
175

8	# An inherited key is resolved from the raw pairs, as of the observation time of the row that inherits it
9	
10	## Context and Problem Statement
11	
12	Slice 1 built a bridge with one entity and no relationships. ADR 0002 asserted that one shared
13	bridge is safe because keys inherit along many-to-one edges while measures do not, and said in as
14	many words that the walk had zero edges and the property was asserted rather than exercised. This
15	slice is the first with an edge: an order is placed by a customer, and the question groups the
16	freight of an order by the *customer's* country, which exists nowhere on the order.
17	
18	So the generator has to get `customer_key` onto an order row. The engine offers four places to get
19	it from, they do not agree with each other, and the names do not say which is which. A probe built
20	a two-entity model with one relationship, changed a foreign key, and read every object the engine
21	produced. It overturned two things ADR 0002 states as fact.
22	
23	**The relationship view is a *current* view, not a historical one.** ADR 0002 says reading it would
24	lose a row whose foreign key changed. That is not what happens. The macro behind
25	`dab.view_<SRC>_<NAME>_<TGT>` is:
26	
27	```sql
28	rank() OVER (PARTITION BY <SRC>_key, type_key ORDER BY eff_tmstp DESC, ver_tmstp DESC) AS nbr
29	... WHERE nbr = 1 AND row_st = 'Y'
30	```
31	
32	Partitioned by the child, so the child never drops out — it is re-pointed. After the probe moved
33	CH1 from P1 to P2, the pair table held both rows with `row_st = 'Y'` and the view held `CH1|P2`
34	alone. Nothing is lost; the *old* pair is what is lost, for every row of that child, retroactively.
35	The reason to read the raw pairs is therefore history, not disappearance, and ADR 0002 got the
36	right answer from the wrong mechanism.
37	
38	**`view_<entity>_with_rel` does carry relationship keys — on the target side, and it fans out.**
39	ADR 0002 says its column list is byte-identical to `view_<entity>`. That is true only for the
40	relationship's *source* entity. Once an entity is a relationship *target*, its `_with_rel` view
41	becomes a double left join through the pair macro and gains the source entity's key **and every one
42	of its attributes**, one row per child. The probe measured the consequence:
43	`sum(CHILD_AMOUNT)` over `view_PARENT_with_rel` returned 200.75 against a true 150.75. That is a
44	live fan trap in a view whose name invites exactly the join that springs it.
45	
46	**`rank()` is not `row_number()`, so a tie returns both rows.** The probe's CH5 had two parent codes
47	in one load, so two pair rows shared an `eff_tmstp`, and the relationship view returned CH5 twice.
48	A child appearing twice in the bridge multiplies its measures — the precise failure the bridge
49	exists to prevent, arriving from the engine's own view rather than from anything we wrote.
50	
51	**The model cannot say that an edge is many-to-one.** This is the finding that decides how the rule
52	is enforced, and it is settled by the engine's own error rather than inferred: adding
53	`cardinality:` to a relationship is rejected with *"Valid fields are: name, definition, description,
54	source, target, source_entity_id, target_entity_id, type"*, and that list is the whole grammar. The
55	one candidate, `type`, is not a cardinality slot — it accepts any string without validation
56	(`1:N`, `MANY_TO_ONE`, `BOGUS_VALUE` all pass `check model`) and is **dropped on compile**: it does
57	not appear in the compiled `model.json` and never reaches the engine. Nor is the engine merely
58	silent about cardinality. It is agnostic by design: it treats a child's parents as a *set*,
59	aggregating all target keys per `(source key, eff_tmstp)` into a fingerprint and writing a row when
60	that set changes. Many-to-many is a supported case, not a defect.
61	
62	So the generator cannot learn "many-to-one" from the model, and it cannot learn it from the data,
63	because the data is legitimately allowed to be many-to-many. Something else has to say it.
64	
65	## Decision Drivers
66	
67	* a measure summed over the bridge is additive at every grain, whatever the model's shape
68	* a bridge row is true as of one instant, and every column on it is true as of that same instant
69	* the generator reads objects whose behaviour has been observed, never ones whose names suggest it
70	* a case the design cannot handle fails the build loudly rather than answering a question wrongly
71	* the walk works for zero edges, one edge and, later, a chain — without a special case per depth
72	
73	## Considered Options
74	
75	* `dab.view_<SRC>_<NAME>_<TGT>` — the engine's ranked relationship view
76	* `dab.v_<SRC>_<NAME>_<TGT>` — the raw pairs plus a relationship name, ranked here
77	* `dab.<SRC>_<TGT>_x` — the pair table directly, with `dab__meta` for the type key
78	* `dab.view_<TGT>_with_rel` — the view named as though it were for this
79	
80	## Decision Outcome
81	
82	Chosen option: **`dab.v_<SRC>_<NAME>_<TGT>`, ranked in the generated SQL as of the child row's own
83	`_observed_at`, one parent per child, with the tie refused by a data check.**
84	
85	`v_<SRC>_<NAME>_<TGT>` is the raw pair table joined to the engine's metadata to add a `rel_name`
86	column, with no ranking and no `row_st` filter. That is what makes it the right source: the pairs
87	arrive unfiltered, and the as-of rule is ours and visible in the generated SQL rather than the
88	vendor's and hidden in a macro. It also solves a naming problem the pair table has on its own — the
89	pair table is named `<SRC>_<TGT>_x` from the *entity pair*, not from the relationship, so two
90	relationships between the same two entities land in one table separated only by a `type_key` whose
91	meaning lives in `dab__meta.atom_contx_desc`. Filtering on `rel_name` says what is meant; filtering
92	on `type_key = 1` says nothing and breaks when a second edge is declared.
93	
94	**As of `_observed_at`, not as of now.** The stage picks a version of the child; the inherited key
95	is the one in force when that version was observed. Today the stage always picks the child's latest
96	version, so this coincides with the current parent and the choice looks free. It is not: it is what
97	keeps the rule stated at the level of a bridge row rather than at the level of a table, so it
98	survives a stage that keeps more than the latest version, which is what a snapshot event and a
99	`_is_current = FALSE` row will both need.
100	
101	So the ranking partitions by the inheriting key **and its observation time**, not by the key
102	alone. A review of this slice caught the first draft doing the latter, which collapses to one
103	parent per key and would hand every retained version of an entity that same parent — "as of now"
104	wearing this rule's clothes, and passing every check because today no stage keeps two versions.
105	The distinction costs one column in a `PARTITION BY` and is the entire difference between the
106	option chosen here and the one rejected.
107	
108	**Exactly one parent per child, and a tie is a build failure.** Since neither the model nor the data
109	can state the cardinality, it is inferred from the mapping and then pinned. The inference is sound:
110	M5 already forbids an attribute expression from containing a subquery, an aggregate or a reach into
111	another table, so a relationship's `target_transformation_expression` reads its own row and is
112	single-valued per staged row *by construction*. What that does not cover is one key appearing on
113	several staged rows of a single load, which is exactly how the probe's CH5 acquired two parents at
114	one instant. So the check is not optional decoration on top of the inference — it is the half of the
115	argument the inference cannot make.
116	
117	The generated SQL uses `row_number()` over `eff_tmstp DESC, ver_tmstp DESC` and then the parent key
118	itself, so it is deterministic and can never emit two rows for one child. `ver_tmstp` is not a
119	formality: the engine writes a closing row that shares its predecessor's `eff_tmstp` and is
120	separated from it only by `ver_tmstp`. Determinism alone would be a silent wrong answer, so a
121	generated check counts children with more than one open parent at the ranking instant and fails the
122	build when it is not zero. The two together mean the bad case is loud, and that if the check is ever
123	ignored the damage is a mis-attributed row rather than a doubled measure. Doubling is worse: it is
124	invisible in both of a question's acceptance queries if both are written the same way.
125	
126	**Only open pairs.** The read filters `row_st = 'Y'`. The engine flips a pair to `'N'` in exactly one
127	case — the source row disappears from `das__staged`, and `FULL_LOG`'s delete branch closes it — and
128	it keeps both rows when it does. In this architecture `das__staged` is an append-only view over
129	parquet, so that should never fire; the filter is there because "should never fire" is not a reason
130	to read a retracted pair if it ever does.
131	
132	`view_<TGT>_with_rel` is refused outright and now for a measured reason rather than an assumed one.
133	The engine's ranked view is refused because its as-of rule is not ours to state and its `rank()`
134	can fan out. The pair table is refused because it cannot name the relationship it is carrying.
135	
136	**A child with no parent keeps its row and inherits a null key.** The probe's CH6 has no pair row at
137	all, so the join is a left join. An order the source attributes to nobody is still an order that
138	was placed, and dropping it would change a count that ADR 0002 already published. Null is not a
139	member: it groups as itself and the generator invents nothing for it, per conventions §1.3.
140	
141	### Corrections to ADR 0002
142	
143	ADR 0002 is not superseded — its decision stands and this record extends it. Two of its factual
144	claims are wrong and are corrected here rather than in place, because what a record was when it was
145	made is the thing that makes it worth keeping:
146	
147	1. "A changed foreign key keeps its row, which reading the relationship view would not have done."
148	   The relationship view does keep the row. It re-points every one of that child's rows at the new
149	   parent and erases the old pair, which is a different defect and a worse one, because it is
150	   invisible.
151	2. "`view_<entity>_with_rel` carries no relationship key columns at all; its column list is
152	   byte-identical to `view_<entity>`." True on the source side only. On the target side it carries
153	   the source entity's key and attributes, fanned out. **ADR 0004 repeats the same claim** —
154	   "`view_<entity>_with_rel` carries no relationship keys despite its name" — and is corrected
155	   here too, not there.
156	
157	A third claim, in this record's own first draft, was corrected a commit later: it was written
158	from a partial reading of the probe that produced it. What that cost is worth naming, because it
159	is the failure mode this whole arrangement is meant to catch — the decision it reached was the
160	one the full report supports, so nothing downstream was wrong, and it was right by luck rather
161	than by reading. The findings it had missed changed how the decision is *enforced*, not what it
162	is.
163	
164	The check ADR 0002 installed for the second claim asserted it of *every* entity, so it fails the
165	moment CUSTOMER becomes a relationship target. That is the check working: it was pinning observed
166	behaviour and the behaviour was mis-observed. It is replaced by one that asserts the real rule —
167	the source side is unchanged, the target side gains exactly the source entity's columns — which is
168	a stronger statement than the one it replaces and would have caught this in slice 1 had it been
169	possible to write then.
170	
171	## Consequences
172	
173	* Good, because the as-of rule is written in the generated SQL, so a reader of `dar/uss/_bridge.sql`
174	  can see when the inherited key was true without reading a vendor macro
175	* Good, because the fan-out the engine's own views expose cannot reach the bridge: the generator
176	  emits `row_number()`, and the case that would have needed it fails the build first
177	* Good, because filtering on `rel_name` keeps two edges between the same two entities in
178	  separate pair objects. It does **not** keep them apart in the bridge, which a review of this
179	  slice caught: a stage carries one key column per entity it inherits from, so two such edges —
180	  or an edge from an entity to itself — would emit that column twice under one name, and DuckDB
181	  resolves the ambiguity instead of raising. The generator refuses both shapes rather than
182	  emitting them. Naming the column after the edge instead of the target would allow them and
183	  would change the bridge's published contract, so it is a decision for the slice that first
184	  needs two, not a shape to guess at now
185	* Good, because the walk is the same shape at zero edges and one, so slice 5's two-hop chain extends
186	  it rather than special-cases it
187	* Bad, because the generated bridge SQL grows a ranked CTE per edge, and at three or four edges it
188	  stops being readable in one screen. It is generated, linted and drift-checked, so this costs
189	  legibility rather than correctness
190	* Bad, because `v_<SRC>_<NAME>_<TGT>` is an engine-internal object with no compatibility promise,
191	  like every other object here. The pinning checks are what turn a vendor change into a failure
192	  instead of an empty column
193	* Bad, and not fixable here: **a foreign key set to null is never retracted.** The engine's reader
194	  filters the pair source on the target key being non-null, so "this child now belongs to nobody" is
195	  inexpressible — re-landing a child with a null parent writes no row, no tombstone and no `row_st`
196	  flip, and the stale pair survives forever. The probe reproduced this. If the source ever nulls an
197	  order's customer, DAB keeps the old customer and nothing says so. That is a property of the
198	  engine, not of this decision; it is recorded here because this is the decision that would
199	  otherwise be blamed for it
200	
201	## More Information
202	
203	The probe found one thing that is not used and should be, when there is a reason to. Every
204	presentation object wraps a DuckDB table macro taking a `p_eff_tmstp` with a default, so the whole
205	DAB layer is point-in-time queryable for nothing: `f_child_parent_x(TIMESTAMP '2026-01-15')` returned
206	the January parent while `f_child_parent_x()` returned the current one. That is a second, shorter
207	way to write the as-of join. It is not taken because it moves the as-of rule back inside a vendor
208	macro, which is the thing this decision is spending SQL to avoid — but a later slice that needs
209	as-of over several objects at once should weigh it again rather than rediscover it.
210	
211	`type_key` is not stable across models: it was 1 for the relationship in this probe and 17 in an
212	earlier one, and attribute type keys differ per entity within a single model. It is never
213	hardcoded — `rel_name` is what the generated SQL matches on, which is the whole reason
214	`v_<SRC>_<NAME>_<TGT>` is read rather than the pair table it wraps.
215	
216	## Confirmation
217	
218	`tests/test_uss.py` asserts the generated bridge left-joins the pairs rather than inner-joining
219	them, that it ranks by `row_number` and not `rank`, that the ranking is as of the child's
220	`_observed_at`, and that a non-owning branch still emits a typed null for a key it does not own —
221	this last one because a union takes its column names from its first branch, so the order of the key
222	columns is the invariant and counting them would not catch a transposition.
223	
224	A generated data check counts children with more than one parent at the ranking instant and must
225	return zero. Another counts bridge rows whose inherited key resolves to no row in the target
226	peripheral, which is the shape a mis-spelled M6 target expression takes: the engine reports nothing
227	at deploy or at execute, and the column is simply null everywhere.
228	
229	The engine-behaviour checks are widened rather than removed: `_focal` and `_idfr` are still empty,
230	`view_<E>_with_rel` is unchanged on a relationship's source side and gains exactly the source
231	entity's columns on its target side.
232	
233	What this slice still does not prove is the fan-out property itself. Both entities here are at the
234	same grain — one order has one customer — so no measure can multiply across the edge no matter how
235	the join is written. The first measure at a finer grain arrives in slice 4, and that is where the
236	test that a parent's measure is not multiplied by its children becomes possible. Saying so is the
237	point: ADR 0002 asserted this property in slice 1 and it is still asserted now.

2	status: accepted
3	date: 2026-09-08
4	decision-makers: [adss maintainers]
5	slice: 4
6	---
7	
8	# The bridge protects a measure and not the attribute it was made from, so a question may not aggregate a peripheral's number
9	
10	## Context and Problem Statement
11	
12	D-0001 puts every process into one shared `dar__uss`, departing from the blueprint's
13	no-cross-dependency rule. Its entire justification, written in slice 1 and carried unexercised
14	through three slices, is that *the fan trap R2 exists to prevent cannot occur in it* — because
15	keys inherit along many-to-one edges and measures do not.
16	
17	Slice 4 is the first slice with two grains, so it is the first that can test that. It half holds.
18	
19	**The measures are safe, structurally, and this is the first demonstration of it.** Over the real
20	two-grain bridge — 830 order rows and 2155 line rows — every shape returns the truth:
21	
22	| query | freight | revenue |
23	|---|---|---|
24	| both measures, whole bridge, no filter, no join | **64,942.69** ✓ | **1,265,793.0395** ✓ |
25	| both, per order month, joined to `_calendar` (3794 rows) | **64,942.69** ✓ | **1,265,793.0395** ✓ |
26	
27	2155 line rows carry `order_key`, and freight does not move. That is what D-0001 has been
28	asserting, and it is now a measurement.
29	
30	**The peripheral is not safe, and the query that breaks it is not exotic.** It is one join — the
31	same join `q01` and `q02` already write:
32	
33	```sql
34	SELECT sum(o.freight_charge)
35	FROM dar__uss._bridge AS b
36	INNER JOIN dar__uss."order" AS o ON b.order_key = o.order_key
37	WHERE b._event = 'ordered';
38	-- 207,306.10 against a true 64,942.69. Once per LINE.
39	```
40	
41	`freight_charge` is a **published column of the order peripheral**. So the rule generalises to
42	something D-0001 never said:
43	
44	> Any `NUMBER` attribute that is also a measure's source appears **twice** in `dar__uss` — once
45	> as an additive measure on its owning stage, protected by a typed null on every other branch,
46	> and once as a plain attribute on its peripheral, protected by nothing. `FREIGHT_CHARGE`,
47	> `SHIP_LAG_DAYS` and `REVENUE` are all in that position.
48	
49	**And it was already live at slice 3, undetected.** On the warehouse as shipped in PR #3, before
50	any line existed, the same query returns **128,897.71** against 64,942.69 — because `ORDER` had
51	two events, so the bridge already had two rows per order. Slice 4 does not introduce the trap. It
52	raises it from 1.98× to 3.19× and makes it reachable from another entity's stage, which is what a
53	fan trap actually is.
54	
55	## Decision Drivers
56	
57	* the property D-0001 rests on is demonstrated or the deviation's argument is not carried
58	* what the demonstration does *not* cover is stated, rather than left for a reader to discover
59	* the trap is kept out of what this system publishes, since it cannot be kept out of SQL
60	* nothing legitimate is removed to achieve it
61	
62	## Considered Options
63	
64	* Stop publishing a numeric attribute on a peripheral when it is also a measure's source
65	* Publish it, and add a query-time rule to the bridge's contract
66	* Publish it, add the rule, **and refuse a question that breaks it**
67	
68	## Decision Outcome
69	
70	Chosen: **the third.** The property is proved for measures, the limit of that proof is written
71	into ADR 0002's contract as a third query-time rule, and a question whose answer query aggregates
72	a peripheral's numeric column is **refused** by the question checker.
73	
74	**Why not remove the column.** A numeric attribute on a peripheral is legitimately useful — it is
75	how a reader filters "orders whose freight was over 100" or sorts a table by it. Removing it to
76	prevent a bad aggregate would break the good use to prevent the bad one, and would make the
77	peripheral a worse description of the entity than the entity has.
78	
79	**Why a rule alone is not enough.** ADR 0002 already publishes two query-time rules and neither
80	covers this one; a third would be true, unread and unenforced. This system's own position, stated
81	in ADR 0006 and ADR 0008, is that a failure which is invisible gets refused where it can be seen.
82	
83	**What can actually be enforced.** Not "no reader writes a bad query" — a bridge does not stop a
84	bad query, it makes the good one natural, and the honest form of that claim is narrower than it
85	sounds. But every number this system *publishes* goes through a question's `uss.sql`, and those
86	are files this repository owns and already checks. So: an answer query may not apply an aggregate
87	to a column of a peripheral. It must aggregate `_measure__…` columns, which are the ones the
88	bridge protects. That is checkable, it is checked, and it stops the trap entering the artefacts
89	anybody reads.
90	
91	The rule has one deliberate hole: a question may still aggregate a peripheral's column if it does
92	so outside `uss.sql`, and a person at a SQL prompt can do whatever they like. That is not a gap
93	this decision can close and pretending otherwise would be the false comfort D-0001 has been
94	running on.
95	
96	### D-0001 does not close
97	
98	Its exit condition, quoted whole, is: *"A second consumer needs isolation: a different shape of
99	the same structure, or a group that must not see part of it."* That has not happened. Slice 4
100	adds a fourth question read by one more persona, and a persona is not a consumer needing
101	isolation — nothing here needs a different shape of the bridge and nothing must be hidden from
102	anybody. Closing the entry now would be closing it for a reason that is not its own exit
103	condition, which is how a register becomes decoration.
104	
105	What changes is the register's **Why**. It has said since slice 1 that the fan trap "cannot occur"
106	in the shared structure. That is true of the measures and false of the peripherals, and the entry
107	now says which, with the number.
108	
109	## Consequences
110	
111	* Good, because the argument D-0001 has been carried on for three slices is measured rather than
112	  asserted, and the measurement is repeated on every build
113	* Good, because the half that does *not* hold is written down with the query that breaks it and
114	  the number it returns, rather than being discovered by somebody trusting the entry
115	* Good, because the trap cannot enter a published answer, which is where it would be believed
116	* Bad, because the refusal is a text rule over SQL, and a sufficiently determined query defeats
117	  it — an aggregate spelled across a subquery, for instance. It raises the cost of the mistake
118	  from zero to deliberate, which is what the other refusals in this system do too
119	* Bad, because a question that genuinely wants a peripheral's number aggregated — "the largest
120	  freight on any order" — now has to model it as a measure. That is more honest and more typing,
121	  and it is the same trade ADR 0008 made
122	
123	## Confirmation
124	
125	`tests/test_fan_out.py` asserts the fan-out property directly, on the neutral fixture's two
126	grains: a parent's measure summed over a bridge containing its children equals the parent's own
127	total, the finer measure is right in the same scan, the coarser measure is null on every finer row
128	while the inherited **key** is not, and — the falsifiable half — the parent's total does not move
129	when a parent gains children. It runs the generated SQL against a warehouse it builds, rather than
130	reading the SQL for substrings, because a substring assertion would pass a generator that emitted
131	the right nulls in the wrong branch.
132	
133	That it can fail is measured rather than assumed. The generator was mutated so a measure inherits
134	along an edge exactly as a key does — carried in the CTE that walks the edge, selected by the
135	stage, and treated as the branch's own. It emits SQL DuckDB accepts, and the four assertions fail
136	together: 402.00 in place of 150.75, three parent measures on the three child rows in place of
137	none, and 904.50 against 402.00 when five children are added to a parent whose size did not
138	change. A fifth test — the peripheral trap below — passes under that mutation, which is correct:
139	the mutation is in the bridge and the trap is not.
140

    22	## Entry format
    23	
    24	Entries are appended in the order they are decided and never removed. A resolved deviation is
    25	marked resolved, with the date and the commit or ADR that resolved it, because the history of why
    26	something looked necessary is worth as much as the fact that it no longer is.
    27	
    28	Field by field:
    29	
    30	* **Rule deviated from** — quote or link the exact rule. "The spirit of layering" is not a rule;
    31	  a row in a blueprint table is.
    32	* **Why** — the constraint that made the conforming option unworkable *here*. Convenience, time
    33	  pressure and unfamiliarity are not constraints; they are reasons to do it properly.
    34	* **Cost** — what this buys the system in trouble. Name the first thing that will break, who pays
    35	  for it, and which future change it makes more expensive. A deviation with no cost is evidence
    36	  the rule is wrong, so supersede the rule instead of deviating from it.
    37	* **Exit condition** — the observable thing that has to become true for the deviation to be
    38	  removed. "When we have time" is not observable.
    39	* **ADR** — the decision record that argued it. Every deviation has one; the register is the
    40	  index, the ADR is the argument.
    41	* **Status** — `open` while it stands, `resolved` once it is gone.
    42	
    43	## Review
    44	
    45	The register is read at the start of every slice. Each open entry is checked against its exit
    46	condition **and against whether its argument is still being carried on assertion**. D-0001 is
    47	what that clause was written for. Its justification rests on measures not multiplying across a
    48	walk over many-to-one edges; slice 2 built the first edge but both its entities were at one
    49	grain, so nothing in the *warehouse* could multiply. That was true and it was not a reason to
    50	wait: the fan-out test runs on the neutral fixture, which gained a second grain in slice 2, so
    51	the proof was available two slices before it was written. Slice 4 measured it, and the same
    52	measurement found that the argument was half wrong — which three slices of re-reading the entry
    53	had not. That is the clause earning its place: an entry can be true, unexamined, and misleading
    54	all at once. An entry should also be re-read the moment a second consumer appears, not only
    55	when isolation is demanded, because by then the shared structure will already have shaped both
    56	readers. An entry whose exit condition has been met and which is still open is a defect in the
    57	same way a failing test is: the system is no longer doing what its own documentation says.

-- Generated from dab/model.yaml and dab/uss.yaml. Do not edit; regenerate.
CREATE OR REPLACE TABLE dar__uss._bridge AS
WITH occurred__version AS (
SELECT
    revision."CHILD_key" AS child_key,
    revision.eff_tmstp AS _observed_at,
    cast(revision."OCCURRED_ON" AS DATE) AS _event_date,
    cast(revision."CHILD_WEIGHT" AS DECIMAL(28, 8)) AS _measure__child__child_weight_children_amount
FROM dab."view_CHILD_hist" AS revision
WHERE revision."OCCURRED_ON" IS NOT NULL
QUALIFY row_number() OVER (
    PARTITION BY revision."CHILD_key"
    ORDER BY revision.eff_tmstp DESC
) = 1
),

occurred__child_points_at_parent AS (
SELECT
    revision.child_key AS child_key,
    revision._observed_at AS _observed_at,
    pair."PARENT_key" AS parent_key
FROM occurred__version AS revision
LEFT JOIN dab."v_CHILD_POINTS_AT_PARENT" AS pair
    ON pair."CHILD_key" = revision.child_key
    AND pair.rel_name = 'CHILD_POINTS_AT_PARENT'
    AND pair.row_st = 'Y'
    AND pair.eff_tmstp <= revision._observed_at
QUALIFY row_number() OVER (
    PARTITION BY revision.child_key, revision._observed_at
    ORDER BY
        pair.eff_tmstp DESC,
        pair.ver_tmstp DESC,
        pair."PARENT_key"
) = 1
),

occurred AS (
SELECT
    revision.child_key AS child_key,
    revision._observed_at AS _observed_at,
    revision._event_date AS _event_date,
    child_points_at_parent.parent_key AS parent_key,
    revision._measure__child__child_weight_children_amount AS _measure__child__child_weight_children_amount
FROM occurred__version AS revision
LEFT JOIN occurred__child_points_at_parent AS child_points_at_parent
    ON child_points_at_parent.child_key = revision.child_key
    AND child_points_at_parent._observed_at = revision._observed_at
)

SELECT
    'child' AS _stage,
    'occurred' AS _event,
    occurred._event_date AS _event_date,
    TRUE AS _is_current,
    occurred._observed_at AS _observed_at,
    occurred.child_key AS child_key,
    occurred.parent_key AS parent_key,
    occurred._measure__child__child_weight_children_amount AS _measure__child__child_weight_children_amount
FROM occurred AS occurred;

260	def relationship_checks(model: Model) -> dict[str, str]:
261	    """One check per way an edge fails without saying so. ADR 0006.
262	
263	    All three failures look identical in the built warehouse -- an inherited key that is null,
264	    or wrong, on rows that look like data rather than like a defect -- and none of them is
265	    reported by the engine at deploy, at execute, or by a question's acceptance queries.
266	    """
267	    generated: dict[str, str] = {}
268	    for edge in model.relationships:
269	        source = model.entity(edge.source_entity_id)
270	        target = model.entity(edge.target_entity_id)
271	        pairs = f'dab."v_{edge.id}"'
272	        open_pairs = (
273	            f"FROM {pairs} AS pair\nWHERE pair.rel_name = '{edge.id}'\n    AND pair.row_st = 'Y'"
274	        )
275	        name = edge.id.lower()
276	
277	        # The generator resolves a tie with row_number(), so it can never fan out -- but
278	        # resolving a tie deterministically is still choosing arbitrarily between two answers.
279	        generated[f"{name}__one_target"] = (
280	            f"{_EDGE}\n"
281	            f"SELECT count(*) AS ambiguities\n"
282	            f"FROM (\n"
283	            f"    SELECT\n"
284	            f"        pair.{crossing(source.source_key)} AS source_key,\n"
285	            f"        pair.eff_tmstp AS observed_at\n"
286	            f"    {open_pairs}\n"
287	            f"    GROUP BY pair.{crossing(source.source_key)}, pair.eff_tmstp\n"
288	            f"    HAVING count(DISTINCT pair.{crossing(target.source_key)}) > 1\n"
289	            f") AS tied;\n"
290	        )
291	
292	        # An edge that loaded nothing is what a mis-spelled M6 source_table looks like: the
293	        # engine skips the relationship in silence and every inherited key is null.
294	        generated[f"{name}__loaded"] = (
295	            f"{_EDGE}\n"
296	            f"SELECT count(*) AS unloaded\n"
297	            f"FROM (SELECT 1 AS declared) AS edge\n"
298	            f"WHERE NOT EXISTS (\n"
299	            f"    SELECT 1\n"
300	            f"    {open_pairs}\n"
301	            f");\n"
302	        )
303	
304	        # And a target expression of the wrong shape loads pairs that join to nothing.
305	        generated[f"{name}__resolves"] = (
306	            f"{_EDGE}\n"
307	            f"SELECT count(*) AS dangling\n"
308	            f"FROM {BRIDGE.sql} AS b\n"
309	            f"LEFT JOIN {Relation(Schema.DAR_USS, target.object_name).sql} AS t\n"
310	            f"    ON b.{target.key_column} = t.{target.key_column}\n"
311	            f"WHERE b._stage = '{source.object_name}'\n"
312	            f"    AND b.{target.key_column} IS NOT NULL\n"

346	def composed_key_checks(
347	    mappings: Sequence[Mapping], contracts: Sequence[Contract]
348	) -> dict[str, str]:
349	    """One check per composite source key: the composition has as many distinct values. ADR 0010.
350	
351	    A separator argument is a prediction about what the parts can hold. This is a measurement
352	    over what actually landed, so a separator that is wrong for this data says so on the build
353	    that loaded it rather than in a report six months later.
354	
355	    The parts are counted as a tuple and the composition as the single value the engine will
356	    key on. Two source rows that compose to one key make the second count smaller, and the
357	    entity that disappears takes its measures with it.
358	    """
359	    generated: dict[str, str] = {}
360	    for entity, table, contract in _composed(mappings, contracts):
361	        current = Relation(Schema.DAS_STAGED, f"{contract.table}__current")
362	        parts = ", ".join(contract.primary_keys)
363	        composed = table.primary_keys[0]
364	        # Named for the entity AND the table. Keyed on the entity alone, an entity
365	        # loaded from two composite tables kept only the last check and reported
366	        # nothing missing -- and `adss check` printed PASS for the one that survived.
367	        generated[f"{entity}__{contract.table}__composed_key"] = (
368	            f"{_COMPOSED}\n"
369	            f"SELECT count(*) AS collisions\n"
370	            f"FROM (\n"
371	            f"    SELECT\n"
372	            f"        count(DISTINCT ROW({parts})) AS parts,\n"
373	            f"        count(DISTINCT {composed}) AS composed\n"
374	            f"    FROM {current.sql}\n"
375	            f") AS counted\n"
376	            f"WHERE counted.parts != counted.composed;\n"
377	        )
378	    return generated

384	def _dated_elsewhere(model: Model, uss: Uss) -> list[tuple[Event, Event, Entity]]:
385	    """Every event that inherits its date, paired with the event that owns that date.
386

388	    inherited date against, and a check that re-derives what it expects from the generator

391	    """

393	    for event in uss.events:
394	        inherited, attribute_id = event.dated_by
395	        if inherited is None:
396	            continue
397	        owner = next(
398	            (
399	                candidate
400	                for candidate in uss.events
401	                if candidate.entity_id == inherited and candidate.dated_by == (None, attribute_id)
402	            ),

417	def inherited_date_checks(model: Model, uss: Uss) -> dict[str, str]:
418	    """One check per inherited date: it agrees with the stage that owns that date. ADR 0009.
419	
420	    The date and the key are resolved in one CTE at one instant, and the two ways that breaks --
421	    resolving the date at a different instant than the key, or against a different version of the
422	    parent -- are both invisible in the warehouse. The parent's own stage carries the same date
423	    through a different code path, so comparing them is independent rather than circular.
424	
425	    What it does not see: a row dropped because its inherited date did not resolve. ADR 0009
426	    makes such a row absent by construction, and an absent row disagrees with nothing. Nothing in
427	    the model says how many rows a stage should have, so there is no honest count to check it
428	    against; the record says so rather than implying this covers it.
429	    """
430	    generated: dict[str, str] = {}
431	    for event, owner, entity in _dated_elsewhere(model, uss):
432	        generated[f"{event.name}__inherited_date"] = (
433	            f"{_INHERITED}\n"
434	            f"SELECT count(*) AS disagreements\n"
435	            f"FROM {BRIDGE.sql} AS inheriting\n"
436	            f"INNER JOIN {BRIDGE.sql} AS dating\n"
437	            f"    ON dating.{entity.key_column} = inheriting.{entity.key_column}\n"
438	            f"    AND dating._event = '{owner.name}'\n"
439	            f"WHERE inheriting._event = '{event.name}'\n"
440	            f"    AND inheriting._event_date != dating._event_date;\n"
441	        )
442	    return generated

463	def measure_checks(uss: Uss) -> dict[str, str]:
464	    """One check per measure: it is non-null on its own event's rows and on no other. ADR 0012.
465	
466	    This is the property D-0001 rests on, carried into every build. `tests/test_fan_out.py`
467	    proves it with numbers on a warehouse it builds; this asserts the mechanism on the warehouse
468	    that was actually built, where a wrong number would be believed.
469	
470	    By EVENT and not by stage. Two events on one entity share a stage, so a per-stage check would
471	    let one event's measure sit on another event's row and report nothing -- and that is the
472	    likelier defect, since every branch of the union comes off the same stage's CTE.
473	
474	    It counts leaks only. A measure that is null everywhere would pass here, and is not this
475	    check's to catch: a bridge that lost its rows disagrees with the source, which is what
476	    `adss check` compares on every build.
477	    """
478	    return {
479	        f"{column.removeprefix('_')}__isolated": (
480	            f"{_MEASURE}\n"

8	# A stage may be dated by a date it inherits along the walk, named where it is inherited from
9	
10	## Context and Problem Statement
11	
12	Slice 4 asks for revenue per order **month**. Revenue is measured on an order line — quantity
13	times price less discount — so the bridge needs a row per line. And **an order line has no
14	date.** The source's `OrderDetail` has five properties and not one of them is a date; the live
15	`$metadata` says so, and there is nothing to map from.
16	
17	The generator can only date a stage by an attribute of the event's own entity. `read_uss`
18	resolves `date_attribute` against `model.entity(event.entity_id)`, so naming the order's date on
19	a line event fails with a bare `KeyError: "ORDER_LINE has no attribute 'PLACED_ON'"` — not even a
20	`UssError`, so the refusal arrives with no explanation attached.
21	
22	Nor may any layer go and fetch one. M1 forbids a join or a subquery in a mapping's `table:`; M5
23	forbids a reach into another table; a DAS contract has no key for a join. A second mapped table
24	on `ORDER_LINE` would be keyed by the order, which is not a line.
25	
26	So the question the plan wrote down for this slice cannot be built at all without deciding
27	something the plan did not anticipate.
28	
29	**What is already true, and is the whole reason this is small.** The walk exists. For every
30	edge, `_inherit_cte` already resolves the parent **as of the observation time of the row that
31	inherits** and puts the parent's key on the child's bridge row. ADR 0006 spent its whole decision
32	on getting that instant right. A date is another column of the row the walk already found.
33	
34	This is also what a Unified Star Schema does. Puppini's bridge is a row per measurement event;
35	the event for an order line is the order being placed, on the day it was placed. Dating a line by
36	its order's date is not an accommodation — it is what the shape means.
37	
38	## Decision Drivers
39	
40	* the question is answerable at all, which today it is not
41	* a bridge row is true as of one instant, and every column on it is true as of that same instant
42	* a mechanism that already exists, extended, rather than a second one beside it
43	* the date a reader sees is traceable to a definition in the one place data is explained
44	* slice 5 walks two hops, and must not need a third mechanism
45	
46	## Considered Options
47	
48	* **(a)** The date inherits along the walk, named as `<ENTITY>.<ATTRIBUTE>` in the sidecar
49	* **(b)** Record `OrderDetails?$expand=Order` so the landed line carries the order's date
50	* **(c)** Give `ORDER_LINE` its own date attribute, mapped from the order via the source
51	* **(d)** Drop the calendar and let the question group on the order peripheral's date
52	
53	## Decision Outcome
54	
55	Chosen: **(a), the date inherits along the walk**, written in `dab/uss.yaml` as
56	
57	```yaml
58	    - id: ORDERED
59	      entity: ORDER_LINE
60	      date_attribute: ORDER.PLACED_ON      # qualified: inherited along the edge to ORDER
61	```
62	
63	An unqualified `date_attribute` still means an attribute of the event's own entity, which is
64	every event declared so far and stays the ordinary case. A qualified one names the entity the
65	date is inherited from, and that entity must be reachable along a declared edge from the event's
66	entity — otherwise it is refused, by name, with the edges that do exist listed.
67	
68	The date is resolved **in the same CTE and at the same instant as the key**, because they are the
69	same row of the same parent. Anything else would put two instants on one bridge row, which is the
70	confusion ADR 0006 calls the entire difference between the option it chose and the one it
71	rejected. A line whose order cannot be resolved gets a null date and therefore no bridge row, by
72	the filter the generator already emits — consistent with how an event that did not happen is
73	already handled.
74	
75	**Why not (b), expanding the source record.** It is the cheap-looking one and it is the worst.
76	`PLACED_ON` would then have two homes — the order's own attribute and a copy on every line — and
77	B8 says a definition exists exactly once. Two homes is how two reports start disagreeing, and
78	this one would disagree *silently*, because both copies come from the same load and would agree
79	until the first time they did not. It also needs a new contract key and a new `Endpoint` field to
80	build a URL the recorder cannot currently express.
81	
82	**Why not (c), a mapped date on the line.** Same objection with an extra step: the mapping would
83	have to reach into another table to get it, which M5 forbids outright.
84	
85	**Why not (d), grouping on the peripheral.** The stage still needs a non-null date to exist at
86	all, so it does not escape the problem. And ADR 0007 rejected the peripheral-as-of-now reasoning
87	already: a peripheral is current state, a bridge row is the version in which the event is dated,
88	and reading one against the other puts two instants on one answer.
89	
90	### What this does not become
91	
92	The temptation this record exists to close is to let `date_attribute` take an expression, or to
93	let it reach further than one declared edge because "the walk goes there anyway". Neither. The
94	value is *a date attribute of an entity reached along a declared edge*, resolved exactly as its
95	key is resolved. Arithmetic on it belongs in the mapping under ADR 0007; anything else is a
96	second expression language in a file that is not linted, which ADR 0007 refused on §3.
97	
98	## Consequences
99	
100	* Good, because the question is answerable, and answerable at the grain it is asked at
101	* Good, because it reuses the walk rather than adding a mechanism beside it: one more column off
102	  a row the generator already resolves, at an instant it already got right
103	* Good, because slice 5's two-hop chain inherits this unchanged — a date reached along two edges
104	  is the same rule applied twice, and needs no new decision
105	* Good, because the date on a line is traceable to `ORDER.PLACED_ON`, which has one definition,
106	  so the page's glossary can explain the axis a reader is looking at
107	* Bad, because `dab/uss.yaml` now has two shapes for one field, and a reader has to know that a
108	  dot means "inherited". The alternative — always qualifying — would rewrite three existing
109	  declarations for no gain, and `<ENTITY>.<ATTRIBUTE>` is the notation the questions already use
110	* Bad, because a line's date now moves if its order is re-pointed to a different order, which
111	  cannot happen in this source and is a real property of the design rather than a bug. The
112	  as-of resolution is what bounds it: the date is the one in force when the line was observed
113	
114	## Confirmation
115	
116	`tests/test_uss.py` asserts that a qualified `date_attribute` is resolved from the inherited
117	entity and not from the event's own; that it is refused, naming the available edges, when the
118	entity it names is not reachable along one; that an unqualified one still means the event's own
119	entity; and that the date and the key come from the same CTE, so no bridge row can carry two
120	instants. A sidecar beside the neutral fixture gains an event on `CHILD` dated by
121	`PARENT.HAPPENED_ON`, which is
122	the shape this record is about and which the fixture did not have. Its SQL is linted with every
123	other emitter's and executed by `tests/test_inherited_date_sql.py`, which builds a parent with
124	more than one version -- the real warehouse has exactly one per key, so the real warehouse
125	could not have shown either of the two defects that test was written for.
126	
127	A generated data check asserts that every bridge row of such a stage carries the same
128	`_event_date` as the stage that **owns** that date, for the key on that row — 2,155 comparisons on
129	the real build. It is independent rather than circular: the parent's own stage gets the date from
130	its version CTE and the child's from its inherit CTE, so resolving the date at a different instant
131	than the key, or against a different version of the parent, shows up here. Both of those are
132	invisible in the warehouse otherwise. `tests/test_inherited_date_check.py` runs it against a
133	bridge built to fail it.
134	
135	A check is generated only where the entity the date comes from has an event on that same
136	attribute. Without one there is nothing independent to compare against, and a check that
137	re-derives what it expects from the generator agrees with a broken generator.
138	
139	**This section previously claimed that check existed.** It did not: nothing in `src/adss/checks.py`
140	emitted it and no such file was in `checks/`. A security review found the claim, and it is the
141	third confirmation in this repository to name a check that could not do what it said — which is
142	why the rule about running the mutation before writing the sentence now lives in the adss skill.
143	
144	What is **not** confirmed, and is recorded rather than claimed: a row dropped because its
145	inherited date did not resolve. This decision makes such a row absent by construction, and an
146	absent row disagrees with nothing. Checking that would need a count of the rows a stage *should*
147	have, and nothing in the model states one — a line whose order has no date is legitimately absent,
148	and no check can tell that from a line the generator lost.

# An ingest is one observation, so every contract it lands shares one clock

## Context and Problem Statement

DAB's history is dated by when DAS observed the row. Northwind's `$metadata` has eleven entity
types and about seventy properties and not one modified, updated or version column, so the
observation time is the only history this platform can honestly claim — and `extracted_at` is
`to_timestamp(cast(_dlt_load_id AS DOUBLE))`, the loader's own clock, so the partition key and the
history clock derive from one fact rather than from two.

**One fact per contract.** `land()` creates one pipeline per contract and `das ingest` runs them
one after another, so a single ingest produces one `_dlt_load_id` per contract, each a fraction of
a second after the last. Measured on a clean rebuild:

| contract | `extracted_at` |
|---|---|
| `customers` | 06:40:43.517150 |
| `order_details` | 06:40:43.916979 |
| `orders` | 06:40:44.199092 |

Contracts are landed in `sorted()` order, so `order_details` always precedes `orders`. Always: the
underscore sorts before `s`, and the loader's id is the wall clock at `pipeline.run()`.

Slice 4 is the first slice that reads one entity's history *as of another entity's observation*.
ADR 0009 resolves an inherited date off the parent version in force when the child was observed:

```sql
LEFT JOIN dab."view_ORDER_hist" AS dated
    ON dated."ORDER_key" = pair."ORDER_key"
    AND dated.eff_tmstp <= revision._observed_at
```

`revision._observed_at` is `order_details.extracted_at`. `dated.eff_tmstp` is
`orders.extracted_at`. They are 0.28 seconds apart, in the wrong direction, so **no ORDER version
precedes any ORDER_LINE row**, the date resolves to null for every line, and ADR 0009's own rule —
a row whose inherited date does not resolve gets no bridge row — removes all 2,155 of them. The
`ordered` stage is empty and q04 returns nothing against the source's 23 rows.

**It was green here for a reason that is not a reason.** This working tree's lake is gitignored
and had accumulated: sixteen `orders` loads, twelve of them older than the earliest
`order_details` load. `view_ORDER_hist` holds exactly one version, from the first of those, at
22:11 the previous day — because `FULL_LOG` writes a new version only when the row changes, and
the recording never changes. That single old version satisfies the `<=`, and it carries the same
`PLACED_ON` any newer one would. A lake that accumulates across runs is a machine for turning a
broken build green.

The bug is not the `<=`. ADR 0006 and ADR 0009 are right that the parent must be resolved as of
the child's observation. The bug is that "the observation" is not one time.

## Decision Drivers

* an as-of join between two entities must not depend on the order their contracts were landed in
* the fix belongs where the fact is wrong, not where the fact is read

* the fix belongs where the fact is wrong, not where the fact is read
* DAS may not learn what DAB's relationships are; the flow runs one way
* what a clean clone builds is what the repository claims, or the claim is worthless

## Considered Options

* **One clock per ingest** — every contract landed by one `adss das ingest` gets one `extracted_at`
* **Land contracts in dependency order** — sort parents before children
* **Fall back to the parent's earliest version** when none precedes the child
* **Compare dates rather than instants** in the as-of join

## Decision Outcome

Chosen: **one clock per ingest.** `das ingest` takes the time once and every contract it lands
carries it, so `extracted_at` says when the *system* observed the source rather than when a
particular pipeline happened to start. `<=` is then satisfied by equality and the as-of join is
independent of landing order.

This is a decision about meaning, not a workaround. Rows fetched by one run of one command are one
observation of one source. Dating them individually says the business changed between two HTTP
calls, which nothing here can know and nothing downstream should have to reason about.

`extracted_at` becomes an explicit column landed beside the payload, rather than a derivation from
`_dlt_load_id`. That is the same number of clocks the spike argued for — "record the source once;
one fact, in two shapes, never two clocks" — restored. What exists today is three clocks, one per
contract, which the spike's own rule already forbade and nobody noticed because nothing compared
them until now.

**Why not land in dependency order.** It would fix the direction and not the cause: two contracts
would still carry two times, so a partial ingest, a retry, or any future check comparing
observation times across entities would break the same way. It also requires DAS to know which
entity is a parent of which, and that is DAB's knowledge — the layer whose whole purpose is to be
independent of where the data came from would have to be consulted by the layer that fetches it.
That is the flow rule, backwards, to fix a clock.

**Why not fall back to the earliest version.** It changes what "as of" means, so a parent this
system genuinely had not yet observed would be resolved against a version from its future. It also
fixes one query rather than the fact, and the next as-of comparison would need the same patch.

**Why not compare dates.** A load spanning midnight breaks it, and the answer to "these two
instants are wrongly ordered" is not "look at them less closely".

### What this does not change

`extracted_on`, the hive partition key, is still the loader's own date, and the existing clock
check still asserts it equals `cast(extracted_at AS DATE)` in UTC. The two can now disagree only
if a load starts before midnight and writes after it, which is the case that check was written for.

## Consequences

* Good, because an as-of join between two entities means what it says, and does not depend on the
  alphabetical order of contract file names
* Good, because a clean clone builds what this repository claims it builds — which was not true of
  slice 4 as first committed
* Good, because the rule generalises: every future comparison of observation times across entities
  is now comparing one fact to itself
* Bad, because two contracts landed by two separate commands still carry two times, correctly —
  they are two observations — so a reader who splits an ingest gets history that says so. That is
  the honest answer and it is still a surprise waiting for somebody
* Bad, because `extracted_at` is now a column this layer writes rather than one it derives, so a
  source field named `extracted_at` is refused where before it was merely shadowed. It was already
  reserved, so nothing changes in practice
* Bad, because the local lake that hid this is still there and still accumulates. Nothing here
  makes a stale lake fail; CI's clean checkout is what says the build is real

## Confirmation

`tests/test_das_round_trip.py` lands two contracts in one ingest, in the order that broke this —
the child's contract first — and asserts every row of both carries the same `extracted_at`, and
that the second landed is not later than the first. It fails on the previous derivation.

The measurement above is repeatable: a clean tree with no `das/lake/` builds an empty `ordered`
stage before this change and 2,155 rows after it, and `adss check` reports `q04: the source and the
star schema agree` in the second case only. CI does exactly that on every push — checkout, build,
check — with no lake, so the clean rebuild is the standing test rather than something anybody has
to remember to run.

**A correction to the Consequences above, which were written before the code.** They say nothing
here makes a stale lake fail. Building it showed otherwise, twice over. A load landed before this
change has no `extracted_at` column at all, `union_by_name` reads it back as null, and DAB then
historizes on a null clock — which surfaced as three duplicate-version findings naming FULL

# Architecture decision records

One file per decision, numbered, in [MADR](https://adr.github.io/madr/) format. A record is
**superseded by a new file, never edited**, because the value of a decision record is the record
of what was true when it was made. A claim that turns out to be wrong is corrected in the record
that found it wrong, named and quoted, rather than quietly rewritten where it stands — ADR 0006
corrects two of ADR 0002's.

**The Confirmation section is the one exception**, because it is not a record of anything: it is a
claim about which checks exist *now*, and a stale one is a lie about the present rather than an
honest account of the past. It is edited to match the checks, and only ever to match them. Twice
already it had drifted the other way — describing a check somebody meant to write.

An ADR lands **before** the code it decides. A decision record written afterwards records what
was built, not what was decided.

-- The answer, from the generated star schema. This is what the destination reads.
SELECT

    cast(sum(b._measure__order__freight_orders_amount) AS DECIMAL(28, 8))

FROM dar__uss._bridge AS b
INNER JOIN dar__uss._calendar AS cal ON b._event_date = cal.date_key
LEFT JOIN dar__uss.customer AS cu ON b.customer_key = cu.customer_key
WHERE b._event = 'placed'
GROUP BY cal.quarter_label, cu.based_in_country
ORDER BY order_quarter, customer_country
